query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a controlled amount of titanium to the equiatomic CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy will promote the in‐situ formation of a thin, thermally stable, low-shear oxide (or oxide/precipitate) layer during sliding, thereby reducing both the coefficient of friction and the wear rate consistently from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy in a single-phase (likely FCC) solid-solution state without any intentional secondary phases.
generation.intervention: Incorporate a minor Ti addition (e.g., by substituting or adding ~5 at.% Ti) into the CoCrFeNi alloy composition to form a modified alloy (CoCrFeNiTi) that can form Ti-rich oxides or precipitates upon sliding.
generation.conditions: Reciprocating sliding tests under ambient (oxidizing) atmosphere performed at temperatures from ~25 °C to 800 °C and under moderate loading typical for tribological evaluations.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of fine, coherent Ti-rich oxide precipitates (or a continuous oxide film) at the sliding interface that is self-healing during operation.
generation.mechanism: The titanium addition is expected to encourage the nucleation of a protective, low-shear Ti-oxide (or mixed oxide) film during sliding at high temperatures. This film acts as a solid lubricant, reducing direct metal-to-metal contact and suppressing abrasive wear, while at lower temperatures the microstructure remains largely unaltered, preserving low friction behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the base CoCrFeNi alloy, the Ti-modified alloy will exhibit a lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate over the entire temperature range. At elevated temperatures, the self-forming oxide film minimizes adhesion and abrasive wear, while at room temperature the mechanical characteristics are maintained.
generation.baseline: The original CoCrFeNi alloy, which under sliding conditions shows higher friction and wear at elevated temperatures due to the absence of a stabilizing, protective oxide layer.
generation.boundary: Results are applicable under atmospheric (oxidative) conditions with moderate loads in a sliding tribometer setup, covering temperatures from room temperature (~25 °C) to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal Ti content for balancing oxide formation and mechanical integrity, as well as the long-term stability and regeneration behavior of the protective oxide film under cyclic wear, remain to be precisely determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (a) base CoCrFeNi alloy and (b) Ti-doped CoCrFeNi alloy with the proposed Ti content. Subject both sets to reciprocating sliding tests under identical conditions at multiple temperatures (e.g., 25 °C, 400 °C, and 800 °C) in an ambient atmosphere. Analyze the wear surfaces using microscopy and surface spectroscopy to detect the presence and composition of oxide films.
measurements: Coefficient of friction as a function of temperature
Surface chemical analysis (e.g., XPS, SEM/EDS) to identify oxide layer formation and morphology
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ti-doped alloy does not exhibit a statistically significant reduction (e.g., >15%) in both friction coefficient and wear rate across the test temperatures compared to the base alloy, or if no stable, continuous Ti-rich oxide film is detected on the sliding surfaces, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 .
